title: The Journey to the Great Oz, part 4
attribution: From The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum (1900), via Project Gutenberg, in reading order.
body: “I’m not surprised that you are,” returned Dorothy. “They must be dreadful beasts.”
The Lion was about to reply when suddenly they came to another gulf across the road. But this one was so broad and deep that the Lion knew at once he could not leap across it.
So they sat down to consider what they should do, and after serious thought the Scarecrow said:
“Here is a great tree, standing close to the ditch. If the Tin Woodman can chop it down, so that it will fall to the other side, we can walk across it easily.”
“That is a first-rate idea,” said the Lion. “One would almost suspect you had brains in your head, instead of straw.”

The Woodman set to work at once, and so sharp was his axe that the tree was soon chopped nearly through. Then the Lion put his strong front legs against the tree and pushed with all his might, and slowly the big tree tipped and fell with a crash across the ditch, with its top branches on the other side.

They had just started to cross this queer bridge when a sharp growl made them all look up, and to their horror they saw running toward them two great beasts with bodies like bears and heads like tigers.
“They are the Kalidahs!” said the Cowardly Lion, beginning to tremble.
“Quick!” cried the Scarecrow. “Let us cross over.”

So Dorothy went first, holding Toto in her arms, the Tin Woodman followed, and the Scarecrow came next. The Lion, although he was certainly afraid, turned to face the Kalidahs, and then he gave so loud and terrible a roar that Dorothy screamed and the Scarecrow fell over backward, while even the fierce beasts stopped short and looked at him in surprise.

But, seeing they were bigger than the Lion, and remembering that there were two of them and only one of him, the Kalidahs again rushed forward, and the Lion crossed over the tree and turned to see what they would do next. Without stopping an instant the fierce beasts also began to cross the tree. And the Lion said to Dorothy:

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why could the Lion not leap the second gulf?
options: It was too broad and deep
His legs were too tired
The Kalidahs were watching him
The edge would not bear his weight

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what was the Scarecrow's plan for the second gulf?
options: Chop down a tree to fall across it
Build a raft to float them over
Fill the gulf with branches and leaves
Follow it until it grew narrower

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who pushed the tree over?
options: The Lion
The Tin Woodman
The Scarecrow
All of them together

questions.prompt: Per the passage, in what order did they cross the tree?
options: Dorothy, the Tin Woodman, then the Scarecrow
The Scarecrow, Dorothy, then the Tin Woodman
The Lion first, then the others together
The Tin Woodman first, with his axe ready

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Lion do when he saw the Kalidahs?
options: Began to tremble
Sprang across the gulf
Attacked them at once
Hid behind the tree

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what did the Lion's roar achieve?
options: It stopped the Kalidahs short in surprise
It drove the Kalidahs back into the forest
It brought the tree down across the ditch
It frightened the Kalidahs into fighting each other

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did the Kalidahs come on again?
options: They were bigger, and two against one
They had not understood the roar
They were hungry and would not be stopped
They knew the Lion was a coward

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Lion's behaviour at the tree show?
options: He turned to face them although he was afraid
He was braver than he had ever admitted
He ran across before the others had gone
He had no fear of the Kalidahs at all

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does the Lion mean by calling it a first-rate idea?
options: An excellent one
A dangerous one
A simple one
A familiar one

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the passage?
options: A bridge is made and crossed with the Kalidahs close behind
The Kalidahs are driven off by the Lion's roar alone
The party decides to fight the Kalidahs at the ditch
The Tin Woodman's axe breaks and the plan fails

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Lion say about the Scarecrow's plan?
options: That one would almost suspect he had brains
That it would take far too long to do
That the tree would never reach across
That he had thought of it himself first

questions.prompt: Per the passage, how sharp was the Tin Woodman's axe?
options: Sharp enough to chop the tree nearly through at once
Too blunt to cut anything but small branches
Sharp, but the tree took him all afternoon
So sharp that it split the tree in two

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did Dorothy do when the Lion roared?
options: Screamed
Fainted
Laughed
Ran back across the tree

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what happened to the Scarecrow at the sound of the roar?
options: He fell over backward
He dropped the basket
He ran on ahead alone
He lost his hat in the ditch

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, how did the party come to meet the Kalidahs just then?
options: They had just started to cross the fallen tree
They had gone looking for them in the forest
The Lion's roar had drawn them to the spot
The beasts had been following since the first ditch

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that they looked up to their horror?
options: With sudden dread at what they saw
With great curiosity
With relief that help had come
With anger at the interruption

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarises the passage?
options: A felled tree gets them over, but the danger follows them onto it
A felled tree proves too short to reach the other side
The Lion drives off two beasts and is praised for his courage
The party argues about whether to cross or to fight
